    About this map

    A style study for the project's Bible maps, in the manner of the Eilers Sunday School wall maps (A. H. Eilers & Co., St. Louis). No Eilers Map No. 6 is known to us, so this sheet fills the number with the empires of the exile.

    What we kept from Eilers

    • Flat tints for each land, with the seas left as paper
    • Water lines along the coasts, and hachured relief
    • Each journey in its own color, with the places numbered
    • A "?" after places whose location is uncertain
    • A grid with an index of places keyed to it

    What we changed

    • Labels never overlap. More appear as you zoom in.
    • Type is never smaller than 11 pixels on screen
    • Borders are drawn as lines as well as tints, so they don't depend on color
    • One sheet shows three empires: choose Assyria, Babylon or Persia from the title or under Layers

    How it was made

    • Land, water and relief come from elevation data; the rivers and lakes from Natural Earth, leaving out modern reservoirs.
    • The journeys follow 2 Kings, Jonah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Ezra and Nehemiah. Every place is named in the verse given, and the build checks each name against this project's translation. The roads between are reconstructions, so they are dashed.
    • Empires are approximate, grown from their cities, and their borders moved within each period. Provinces and vassals have their own tints inside an empire's border.
    • Places are the towns named in the Old Testament that OpenBible.info can locate. Places scored at least 300 are shown; those below 500 out of 1,000 are marked "?".
    • Names are spelled as in this project's Open Plain English Translation.

    Sources

    • Places: OpenBible.info Bible Geocoding Data, CC BY 4.0
    • Elevation: AWS Terrain Tiles (SRTM, GMTED2010, ETOPO1)
    • Style: the Eilers Sunday School wall maps, published before 1931
    • Rivers and lakes: Natural Earth (public domain)

      Index of places · Map No. 6

      Grid squares are two degrees of latitude and longitude: letters across the top, numbers down the side. A "?" marks a place whose location is uncertain.
